Client Work · via ProSense

Salad · Adelanto de Nómina

A payroll-advance acquisition flow for Novacard's Mexican market, delivered through ProSense. Shipped in one month against a three-to-six-month estimate, then proven with a live four-variant test on paid traffic.

Product Manager Novacard · via ProSense Aug 2026 · 1 month Visit the live page ↗

The Problem

Payroll advance is a category where the decision takes minutes and trust is the only real barrier. The Mexican market already had minu.mx and platacard.mx competing on speed, with Dave, Brigit and EarnIn setting user expectations globally. Novacard needed an acquisition flow that converted cold, paid traffic into completed applications without the user ever speaking to a human.

My Role

Product manager, from discovery to launch: wrote the PRD from scratch through structured stakeholder interviews, directed the design with written rationale for each decision, built the prototypes on the existing design system, and ran the post-launch analytics myself. The triage one-pager and the PRD for this launch are shown in the AI-Assisted PRD Delivery case.

Constraints That Shaped The Design

  • Advance capped at 10,000 MXN: determined how the calculator framed the offer
  • LFPDPPP, Mexico's data protection law: governed what the form could ask and how consent was captured
  • Full-funnel attribution required: UTM and click_id, with an affiliate route on AppsFlyer OneLink using dynamic click_id injection
  • Multi-team scope with external integrations, originally scoped at three to six months

Decisions & Why

The flow runs hero → calculator → form, deliberately in that order: the user sees their own number before being asked for any data.

I chose the variant that puts real app screens in the "how it works" section. In a category where the fear is "will the money actually arrive," seeing the product removes doubt before anyone types in their details. The final screen carries the same logic: a funds-received notification, not a generic confirmation.

A real customer testimonial replaced a stock crowd photo. Trust in fintech is built on people, not imagery. And a scenario line sits above the headline so the user recognizes their own situation before reading the offer. The Adelanto de Nómina card is also visually prioritized in the "Why Nova" block, above.

Result

Shipped in one month against a three-to-six-month estimate. Four landing page variants ran live on paid traffic from launch. In the first 11 days:

Variant Visits Started Completed Conversion
/391,73848028416.3%
/491,42938323016.1%
/791,46948127919.0%
/991,53947628718.6%
Total6,1751,8201,08017.5%

The best-performing variant converted at 19.0% against 16.1% for the weakest, an 18% relative lift on identical paid traffic, found by testing rather than guessing.

17.5% of paid visits converted to a completed application, well above the 2–5% typical benchmark for cold fintech lead generation. 59.3% of everyone who started the form finished it, directly downstream of the trust decisions above: the product preview, the funds-received screen, the real testimonial.

Personal Project · AI-Assisted Build

Voodoo Village · Weekend Timetable

Voodoo Village is a real festival: Grimbergen, Belgium, 11–13 September 2026, ten stages, dozens of acts across a weekend. I built a personal timetable app for it with Claude: a live now-playing view, search across the whole weekend, and a plan that warns about clashes, all from the festival's published lineup.

Personal project Open the app ↗

The Original

The festival publishes its timetable as a single dense poster image, one per day, like the one above, ten stages packed into a grid, meant to be downloaded and zoomed into rather than read standing in a field. No search, no sense of what's on right now, no way to build a plan across stages or catch two sets that overlap.

What I Built

A single-file web app, installable to a phone's home screen, that turns the same lineup data into something usable on the day:

  • Now: a live view of what's playing on every stage this minute, in Brussels time
  • Grid: the full day as a scrollable timeline across all ten stages
  • Stages: browse set by set, with artist bios and Spotify/SoundCloud/Instagram links where I could find them
  • Mine: star sets to build a personal plan; it flags overlaps and shows the free time between stages
  • Crew: an opt-in check-in so friends can see which stage everyone's at, off by default until it's wired to a backend

Personal Project · AI-Assisted Concept

Ground-Risk Monitoring Concept

A personal concept: a dashboard for tracking borehole depth and contamination trends across a site, built with Claude. The point was to take a technical domain I didn't know and get to a working interface fast.

Personal concept React / Tailwind, then rebuilt standalone

Why This Exists

Ground risk and subsurface data were a new domain for me. I wanted to sit with it and see what a working interface for it could look like, and how quickly I could get there. This is a self-directed concept, not client work.

The Domain

Ground-risk analysis combines geophysical scanning and geotechnical data to de-risk ground conditions for large infrastructure projects, catching problems before they turn into budget overruns. I picked a narrow, concrete slice of it: a dashboard that tracks individual borehole readings and flags which sites need attention.

What I Built

  • A card and map view of every monitored site, with contamination level surfaced at a glance through color coding
  • A detail panel per site with a contamination trend chart across recent samples and a contextual recommendation (routine cycle vs. flag for re-testing)
  • Filtering by risk level, search by site ID, and sorting by depth, risk, or sample recency
  • A self-contained schematic map view plotting sites by relative coordinates, color-coded the same way as the cards

Try It

Real, working demo below: filter, search, switch to the map view, click a site to see its trend.

Honest Framing

Sample data only: coordinates, depths, and contamination readings are illustrative, not from a real survey. It's here to show how I approach an unfamiliar, technical domain and turn it into a working interface fast.

Lead Product Design

Radom · Access Leasing

Access Leasing was Radom Network's marketplace for leasing access to assets and services: mining hardware, cloud servers, APIs, even live sensor data, all paid in crypto on Arbitrum. I led the product design, and the product launched.

Lead Designer Radom Network Web3 · Arbitrum Launched

The Product

Two sides meet in one marketplace. Providers define a lease offer for an asset or service: the token they accept, the price, the minimum and maximum lease period, and, if they want, a whitelist of wallets allowed to buy. Lessees browse the offers, order with a connected wallet, and manage everything they've bought in one place.

My Role

I was the lead designer on Access Leasing and owned every flow in it: the marketplace, creating a lease offer, buying one, and managing or cancelling it afterwards, plus the responsive page templates underneath.

Setting Up a Lease Offer

A provider sets up an offer in one form: pick one of five tokens (USDC, DAI, WETH, USDT, or GUSD) and a price per minute, which the form converts into hourly, daily, monthly, and yearly rates. A toggle turns on buyer whitelisting with a list of approved wallet addresses, and the provider picks the asset or service the lease covers before creating it. On the marketplace, a buyer who isn't on the whitelist sees a note explaining why they can't order.

Try It: Unsubscribing from a Lease

The cancellation flow, clickable. Leaving takes a deliberate confirmation, and ends with a chance to review the lease, so a cancellation still tells the team something.

Click the highlighted spot on the screen, or use Next. Arrow keys work too.

One Layout, Every Breakpoint

The same lease agreements page at 375, 1024, 1280, and 1536 px. I set up the page templates the product was built on, with a layout grid for each breakpoint. On mobile the sidebar gives way to a top bar and the cards stack into one column.

Outcome

Access Leasing launched with the whole lease lifecycle designed, from listing an asset or service to ordering it with a wallet and managing or cancelling it afterwards.

AI-Assisted PRD Delivery

Owned the requirements lifecycle for enterprise clients at ProSense, a digital agency, using an AI-assisted facilitation workflow built on Claude to move faster from stakeholder conversation to a signed-off PRD.

AI Product Manager ProSense (Digital Agency) Jun 2026–Sep 2026 · Remote

The Context

ProSense runs product and requirements work for enterprise clients across industries: telecom and consumer goods, pharma, banking, and fintech. My job was to be the person who turned a stakeholder's intent into a document engineering could actually build from, running the full cycle from first conversation to sign-off.

Clients

Internal projects Novacard Skala-R Rubytech

How the AI-Assisted Workflow Worked

  1. Stakeholder discoveryStructured interviews with client stakeholders to surface real requirements, business constraints, and the "why" behind the ask, not just a feature list.
  2. AI-assisted draftingInterview notes went into a Claude-based facilitation workflow that drafted the one-pager and the full PRD. The first draft came faster, so more of my time went to judgment calls instead of formatting.
  3. One-pager + full PRDEvery engagement produced both a short-form one-pager for quick stakeholder alignment and a full PRD with the requirement-level detail engineering needed.
  4. Client review portalClients commented directly on a dedicated PRD review portal; I triaged every comment and closed the loop in the document itself, so nothing got lost in email threads.
  5. Sign-off & handoffPRDs and requirements were tracked against Jira tickets in a Git-based repo, with structured review before every change landed, then handed off to engineering.

Example: Salad, from Triage to PRD

Every request started with triage: a one-pager that frames the problem, the audience, the metric, and the scope on a single page, and sets a tier that decides how deep the PRD goes. Salad came in as tier L, so it got a full PRD. Both documents are below, with names replaced by roles. They're a snapshot from before launch, so a few numbers differ from what finally shipped.

Names replaced by roles

SALAD (Adelanto de Nómina) · Dummy Site · One-Pager

Author: Elena · Created: August 2026 · Updated: August 2026 · Tier: L (Large)
Problem
Novacard doesn't know whether people in Mexico's open market are ready to move their salary to Novacard for Salad (Adelanto de Nómina), or whether there's strong demand for this kind of credit line. Launching the full product without validation is a high financial and operational risk.
Who it's for
Employed Mexicans earning 9,600–19,000+ MXN, customers of BBVA, Banorte, Santander, Citibanamex, Banco Azteca, Scotiabank, and BanCoppel.
Goal and metric
Test the hypothesis that users are willing to move their salary to Novacard. Visit → completed form conversion ≥ X%; the threshold is an Open question for the product owner (client) before launch.
Solution
A landing page with a hero offer, a limit calculator (min(salary × 40%, 50,000 MXN)), a 4-step application form, and a confirmation screen. No OTP and no hand-off to the app: applications are collected with UTM and click_id into a table and tagged in the LMS.
Out of scope
A/B testing, CRM integration, automatic export to the analytics system, onboarding existing customers, phone OTP verification, hand-off to the mobile app, application scoring and underwriting.
Key dependencies
Novacard LMS (LMS team), marketing analytics (client's marketing), legal (LFPDPPP), design (Figma), tech lead (stack and domain), ad platforms.
Success criterion
Visit → form conversion and funnel data quality are good enough to make an informed call on launching the full product.
Top risks
(1) The conversion threshold that would confirm the hypothesis isn't defined. (2) The LFPDPPP legal copy isn't ready. (3) There's only a prototype so far, not final designs.
Open questions
Conversion threshold (product owner, client), LFPDPPP consent copy (legal), how leads are tagged in the LMS (LMS team), tech stack and domain (tech lead), who analyzes the results (product owner).

SALAD (Adelanto de Nómina) · Dummy Site · PRD

Author: Elena · Created: August 2026 · Updated: August 2026 · Tier: L · Links: designs in Miro and Figma (final version is an open question), tickets TBD, analytics dashboard TBD

1. Context and Rationale

Problem. Novacard plans to enter Mexico's payroll market with Salad (Adelanto de Nómina, a credit limit based on salary). Only banks serve this segment; fintechs don't compete there yet. Before launching the full product, demand has to be validated: are users willing to move their salary from their bank to Novacard in exchange for benefits? The pain today is that there's no data confirming demand, and launching without validation is a high financial and operational risk.

Evidence. Facts (confirmed):

  • Average salary in Mexico is about 19,000 MXN, minimum about 9,600 MXN (source: client meeting, 19 June 2026)
  • Market norm: credit issued doesn't exceed 40–50% of the customer's salary
  • Target source banks: BBVA, Banorte, Santander, Citibanamex, Banco Azteca, Scotiabank, BanCoppel

Hypotheses (not confirmed):

  • Users are willing to move their salary to a fintech in exchange for benefits
  • Novacard's offer (limit, debit card, cashback, and yield) is attractive enough to convert

Every funnel event is sent to the dataLayer through dataLayer.push, and the hypotheses are tested on that data.

Goal and success metric. Test the hypothesis that Mexican users are willing to move their salary to Novacard.

MetricTargetStatus
Visit → completed form conversion≥ X% (threshold TBD)Open question Product owner (client), before launch
Step conversion through the funnel (1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → submit)Diagnose drop-offsNeeds event tagging

Non-goals (deliberately out of scope):

  • A/B testing landing page variants
  • CRM integration
  • Automatic data export to the analytics system
  • Onboarding existing Novacard customers
  • Phone OTP verification
  • Sending users to the mobile app after they apply
  • Application scoring and underwriting

Strategic fit. Salad is the first step in Novacard's entry into Mexico's payroll market. The landing page is a demand-validation tool: its results decide whether the full product is worth launching. Market potential is rated high, and fintechs aren't present in it yet.

2. Solution

Main user flow:

StepAction
1The user lands on the page from an ad (UTM + click_id)
2Sees the hero with the Adelanto de Nómina offer of up to 50,000 MXN and taps “Check My Limit”
3Calculator: enters their salary (slider, 5,000–30,000 MXN) and picks a pay frequency. The system shows the limit: min(salary × 40%, 50,000 MXN)
4Sees the limit and taps “Apply” to go to the form
5Form step 1, Basic info: name, email, phone, city, Novacard customer status
6Step 2, Work: employment type, employer, tenure, industry, how the salary is paid
7Step 3, Income and Nómina limit: salary, pay frequency, current bank, desired advance amount
8Step 4, Transfer and consents: willingness to move the salary, motivation, two required checkboxes
9“Join the Pilot” → confirmation screen “Application submitted”
10Data, UTM, and click_id are saved to a table; the lead is tagged Salad in the LMS

Functional requirements:

  • Landing page: hero, “How it works”, “Why Nova” (5 benefits), calculator, FAQ
  • Calculator: 5,000–30,000 MXN slider, pay frequency, real-time limit using min(salary × 40%, 50,000). CAT 46% / 58% / 87%, service fee 56 / 70 / 105 MXN per 1,000 MXN (weekly / twice a month / monthly)
  • 4-step form with a progress bar, Back and Continue, and a final “Join the Pilot”
  • Client-side validation of every field before moving to the next step
  • After submitting, a confirmation screen with no redirect to the app
  • Form data, UTM, and click_id saved to a table, with CSV export
  • Leads tagged with a tag or field in the Novacard LMS
  • Analytics events at every funnel step (see Data and analytics)

Design. Designs are linked in Miro and Figma; the final version is an open question, and only the SALAD_dummy_v3 prototype exists for now. Changes to the current app screen in the hero: Tarjeta de crédito → Adelanto de Nómina, and the Wallet icon is removed. The first form screen is merged with the calculator and cut down to full name and phone; the other steps are unchanged. Every “Apply” button leads to the form block, with no separate path through the calculator. The FAQ is unchanged.

States and edge cases:

StateBehavior
Salary below 5,000 MXN on the sliderThe slider minimum is 5,000 MXN; no lower limit is shown
40% of salary above 50,000 MXNThe limit shows the 50,000 MXN ceiling
Required field emptyHighlight and error text; moving on is blocked
Invalid email or phoneClient-side format validation with an error message
Double click on submitThe button locks after the first click
Server error on saveError message and an offer to retry; no data is lost
URL without UTMThe form works normally; UTM fields stay empty
Mobile browserFully responsive
Existing Novacard customerThe field records the answer; no special routing is needed in the MVP

Business rules and logic:

  • Limit formula: min(salary_MXN × 0.40, 50,000), calculated client-side in real time
  • Service fee: 56 / 70 / 105 MXN per 1,000 MXN (weekly / twice a month / monthly)
  • CAT (46% / 58% / 87%) is a mandatory regulatory disclosure on the calculator and in the FAQ
  • Both consent checkboxes in step 4 are required to submit
  • “Existing NovaCard customer?” is required; in the MVP it affects analytics segmentation, not routing

Data and analytics (events):

EventTriggerParameters
page_viewLanding page loadsutm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_content, click_id
calculator_openClick on “Check My Limit”none
calculator_resultSlider change (debounced)salary_amount, salary_frequency, calculated_limit
form_startCTA click after the calculatorcalculated_limit

form_submit_successSaved successfullynone
form_submit_errorError on saveerror_code

3. Dependencies and Impact

Impact on what exists. The landing page is a new artifact; the main Novacard site isn't directly affected in the MVP. The LMS needs a field or tag to mark Salad leads: a small change, but it needs sign-off from the LMS team. Salad UTM tags will flow into the shared marketing analytics, so filtering rules have to be agreed with marketing in advance.

Dependencies:

DependencyOwnerWhat's needed
Novacard LMSLMS teamA field or tag for Salad leads, and the data transfer format (campaign UID)
Marketing analyticsClient's marketingUTM scheme for the Salad campaign
Client's legal teamNovacard legalAviso de privacidad (LFPDPPP) and consent copy for step 4
Design teamDesignerFinal designs in Figma
Tech lead and DevOpsTech leadTech stack, domain or subdomain, hosting
Ad platformsMarketingCampaign setup with correct UTM and click_id

Contracts and compatibility. Not applicable: the landing page runs as an isolated instance, with no integration with the main Novacard database.

Impact on adjacent metrics. Salad UTMs could skew Novacard's overall traffic numbers; mitigation: filtering agreed with marketing. Salad leads in the shared LMS funnel could skew the main product's conversion; mitigation: a mandatory Salad tag.

Non-functional requirements. LCP ≤ 2.5 s on mobile, critical for Mexico's mobile-first market. Fully responsive from 320 px, on iOS Safari and Chrome for Android. LFPDPPP compliance, with the aviso de privacidad as a required part of the form. Personal data in secure storage, with CSV export only for authorized staff. Baseline WCAG 2.1 AA. Analytics events retried on failure; data loss isn't acceptable.

4. Delivery and Verification

Acceptance criteria (Given / When / Then). Calculator:

  • Given a salary of 20,000 MXN / When the user moves the slider / Then the limit is 8,000 MXN
  • Given a salary of 30,000 MXN / When the user moves the slider / Then the limit is 12,000 MXN (30,000 × 40%; the 50,000 MXN ceiling can't be reached within the current 5,000–30,000 slider, see the open question below)
  • Given a salary of 5,000 MXN / When the user moves the slider / Then the limit is 2,000 MXN

Form validation:

  • Given “Full name” is empty / When the user taps Continue / Then the field is highlighted and moving on is blocked
  • Given an email without “@” / When the user taps Continue / Then a validation error shows
  • Given neither consent is checked / When the user taps “Join the Pilot” / Then the button is disabled or an error shows

Saving data:

  • Given the form was submitted / When the data is saved / Then the “Application submitted” confirmation screen shows, with no redirect to the app
  • Given the user arrived with ?utm_campaign=salad&utm_source=fb / When the form is submitted / Then those values are saved in the record
  • Given a click_id in the URL / When the form is submitted / Then the click_id is saved

LMS tagging:

  • Given a Salad lead is saved / When the record reaches the LMS / Then it's tagged “Salad” and the client's product owner can filter by it

Scope by phase:

PhaseContent
MVPLanding page (hero, how it works, why Nova, FAQ), calculator, 4-step form with validation, confirmation screen, saving data with UTM and click_id, CSV export, LMS tagging, analytics events, responsive layout, aviso de privacidad
After MVPA/B testing, real-time analytics dashboard, CRM integration, email notification after applying

Rollout and rollback. A separate subdomain or domain, not connected to the main Novacard database (decided with the tech team on 4 June 2026). Launch behind a feature flag, with ad traffic only after QA. Rollback: turn off the flag or change the DNS record, with recovery under 30 minutes and no impact on the main site. Data collected before a rollback is kept and can be exported.

Launch analytics. Results are reviewed at 7 days (operational) and 14 days (the main decision on the hypothesis). Continue if conversion is at or above the threshold, which is still an Open question for the product owner (client). Stop if form save errors exceed 5%, or if conversion is below 50% of the threshold after 7 days. Who analyzes the results is an Open question.

UX Design

eir.ie · Web & Mobile Redesign

Eir is an Irish telecom that wanted its online account to work for older customers: paying a bill, checking usage, and managing a plan without calling support. The existing site wasn't built with this audience in mind, and it showed in low take-up of digital bill pay and self-service.

Senior UI/UX Designer 3-month engagement Web + mobile Remote research (COVID-19) eir.ie ↗

Challenges & Goals

  • Usability: an intuitive, navigable site for users with limited digital experience.
  • Accessibility: designing for varying digital literacy and physical impairments, like reduced vision or dexterity.
  • Engagement: a design that makes older customers want to use the online account, not just put up with it.
  • Time constraint: a three-month window to design and ship.
  • Remote collaboration: research, interviews, and testing all had to run remotely under COVID-19 restrictions.

Try It: Paying a Bill on Mobile

Paying a bill was the task this redesign had to make easy for older customers. These are the real screens, wired up the way the Figma prototype was: the account page scrolls, and what was clickable still is.

Tap anywhere to see what's clickable.

What to try

  1. Let the account load: the customer is greeted by name, not a blank screen.
  2. Scroll the account page, then tap Make a payment.
  3. On the summary, tap Edit to pick another card, or Add another payment method to add one.
  4. Tap Pay now, then Close. The menu at the top right opens My bill and My plan.

Why it works for older customers

  • One number first: the balance, what it includes, and when the direct debit goes out.
  • One clear action per screen, with large tap targets and plain labels.
  • The amount and the card can be changed before paying, and nothing is charged without a final Pay now.
  • The confirmation says what happens next: the payment can take up to 3 business days to show.

The Same Flow on Desktop

On desktop the account is one page of expandable sections, and payments open in a focused dialog on top of it, so customers never lose their place. Expand My bills, open a bill, pay from the balance card, or open the menu.

Click anywhere to see what's clickable.

Process

  1. Research & discoveryStakeholder meetings to align on business requirements, plus remote interviews with a diverse group of elderly users via Lookback and competitive analysis, to ground the approach in real needs rather than assumptions.
  2. Ideation & wireframingVirtual brainstorming sessions with the design team, then low-fidelity wireframes focused on simplicity and clear flow, iteratively refined against stakeholder and early user feedback.
  3. Prototyping & testingHigh-fidelity prototypes taken into remote usability testing sessions; results analyzed for usability issues, preferences, and areas to improve before build.
  4. Implementation & handoffA detailed technical specification for the development team, close collaboration through the build, and final adjustments driven by developer feedback and further user testing.

Research in Practice

The questionnaire had separate sections for desktop and mobile, so each got its own read on the experience. I documented task flows step by step, for example SIM card activation and the Amazon Prime Video offer, so engineering knew exactly what "done" looked like.

Every State, Not Just the Happy Path

The master file went to development with every state designed: a payment that succeeds or fails, a card being verified with the bank, a card approved or declined, an expired card, plus alerts, offers, and bill variants for mobile and desktop.

Beyond Payments

The same patterns carry the rest of the account on desktop: current usage across several accounts, the full payment history, changing the eir TV PIN, and managing the devices signed in to eir TV.

Handoff Details

The client asked for the developer handoff in Google Slides, so that's where it lived: the IA, screen-by-screen flows for mobile and desktop, and the edge cases next to the happy paths. For example, panels that show a spinner while slow data loads, and a greeting that uses the customer's name once it's available and a friendly generic line until then. Every screen came from one Figma master file built on a shared component library.

Outcome

A redesigned, accessible web and mobile account and a complete developer handoff, delivered within the three months. The design came from interviews with the customers the old site served worst, not from internal assumptions about what "simple" means.

Inside the Platform

Try It: Three Directions

UX Design

UX for three.ie

Three is an Irish telecom that sells plans, phones, and accessories online. I mapped the customer journeys for three of its e-commerce epics and ran a heuristic evaluation of the live site, to show the team where buying gets hard and what to change.

UX/UI Designer CJM · Heuristic Evaluation

My Role

I owned the UX work on these epics: aligning business requirements, mapping how customers actually move through the shop, and shaping solutions around the information architecture and what the platform could support.

How I Built the CJM

Each journey map had six layers: objectives (what the customer wants to get done), actions (the steps they take), touchpoints (where they meet Three), pain points (where it gets frustrating), emotions (how they feel at each step), and opportunities (what to change).

User Flows

Some flows needed more detail for stakeholders than a journey map gives, so I drew the current user flows as well. This one follows an anonymous customer through the shop: each blue box is a screen, each diamond is something the customer does.

Pain Points & Opportunities

  • Checkout takes too long. Merge screens so the customer doesn't press a checkout button on several pages, and test whether one delivery-and-review page works better than two.
  • Plan changes stall. Switching from bill pay to prepay, or upgrading a plan, got stuck and the flow stopped. First step: find out whether it's a technical issue.
  • Accessories sit outside checkout. Customers had to leave checkout to find an accessory and come back, or buy it separately from the phone. Suggest accessories on the basket page, and allow one checkout for phone and accessories together.
  • After the order. A new experience where customers track the order, confirm on the web when it arrives, and leave feedback for Three.

Choice of Tools

The work was remote, so I built the maps in Miro rather than a spreadsheet: the team could add stickies, leave comments, and walk through the journeys together.

Heuristic Evaluation

I also evaluated the live site against Jakob Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics. Most of it held up: breadcrumbs and a checkout progress tracker, clear button labels, form validation, and no forced sign-up. The problems were in the details. Page headings didn't match their breadcrumb labels (the Accessories page was titled Your Lifestyle Products), heading sizes and alignment jumped from page to page, and product pages suggested related items but never recently viewed ones.

Marketing Materials

Beyond the UX work, I also designed marketing banners for Three. This one brings customers back to an unfinished basket in the Lifestyle Store, laid out for desktop, tablet, and two phone sizes.

Outcome

After mapping Epics 3, 4, and 5, the team had one view of the critical customer paths and a concrete list of where they broke. My recommendation was to simplify the flows, test the simpler version with customers, and use that data to make the case to stakeholders.

UX Design

apc.com · UPS Selector Flow

APC by Schneider Electric sells uninterruptible power supplies and data center power and cooling equipment in over 150 countries. Its UPS Selector helps customers find the right unit, either by the load they need to cover or by the devices they need to protect. I had two months to rethink it.

Senior UI/UX Designer 2-month engagement Heuristic evaluation UPS Selector ↗

The Challenge

Rethink the UPS selection flow, one of the portal's key tools, in two months and inside APC's existing design system.

My Role

  • Gathered business and user requirements through interviews.
  • Ran a heuristic evaluation of the existing selector.
  • Identified technical limitations together with the development team.
  • Designed wireframes and clickable prototypes.
  • Supported the development team through the build.

The Heuristic Evaluation

Before redesigning, I walked the existing selector through two real use cases: finding a UPS by load (800 W for 1 hour 25 minutes) and by device (a Cisco router in the rack). I rated every problem against Nielsen's 10 heuristics on a three-level severity scale.

65
issues logged
10
major
51
minor
4
cosmetic

Issues by step of the flow

  • Results page17
  • By device, 3 steps12
  • Add options11
  • By load11
  • Compare7
  • Selector entry4
  • Selector pop-up3

The major ones:

  • Dead ends: inaccurate input or extra filters led to an empty results page.
  • No way back: part numbers and Add Options took customers off the results page, and Add Options had nothing but the browser's back button.
  • No final price: the price with the chosen options included was never shown, and no step had a clear call to action.
  • Comparison: hard to read across technical criteria, and impossible to update without starting over.

From Findings to Design

With the problems ranked, I sketched new interface solutions on paper and refined them into digital wireframes and clickable prototypes. I worked inside APC's existing design system throughout, and coordinated with the team whenever a new element had to be introduced, so the system stayed up to date.
